slides.title: What is money?
slides.text: Money is used to buy things you need. You can trade money for a toy or a snack.

slides.title: Money usually comes from work
slides.text: Most money comes from work, like a job. Kids can earn money too, by doing chores.

slides.title: Doing chores to earn money
slides.text: Chores are jobs you do at home, like sweeping or feeding a pet. Doing chores is one way kids can earn money.

slides.title: Some chores pay more than others
slides.text: A big chore, like cleaning a whole room, can pay more than a small chore, like putting away one toy. Bigger jobs often earn more money.

slides.title: Getting an allowance
slides.text: Some kids get a little money each week. This regular money is called an allowance.

slides.title: Counting your money
slides.text: You can count your coins to see how much you have. Counting first helps you know what you can buy.

slides.title: Earning money feels good
slides.text: Money you earn yourself can feel extra special. You worked hard, so you earned it.

slides.title: Keeping your money safe
slides.text: Keeping your money safe means not losing it. A piggy bank or a wallet is a safe place for it.

slides.title: Needs vs. wants
slides.text: A need is something you must have, like food. A want is something nice to have, like a toy.

slides.title: Saving in a piggy bank
slides.text: Saving means keeping money instead of spending it. You can save coins in a piggy bank.

slides.title: Waiting to buy something
slides.text: Sometimes you do not have enough money yet. Waiting and saving a little more can get you there.

slides.title: You can't buy everything
slides.text: You cannot buy every single thing you want. Picking one thing means waiting for another.

slides.title: Comparing prices
slides.text: The same toy can cost different amounts. Checking two stores first can save you money.

slides.title: Sharing and giving
slides.text: You can use money to help other people. Giving someone a gift shows that you care.

slides.title: Choosing at the store
slides.text: At the store, you might only have enough for one thing. Picking your favorite is part of shopping.

slides.title: A small treat or a bigger toy
slides.text: A small treat costs a little and is gone fast. A bigger toy costs more but can last a long time.

slides.title: Ask yourself: need or want?
slides.text: Before you buy something, ask if you need it or just want it. This helps you pick what matters most.

slides.title: What is an allowance?
slides.text: An allowance is money a kid gets regularly, like every week, sometimes for chores and sometimes just for practice. Deciding yourself whether to spend or save it teaches real money skills early.

slides.title: Making a simple budget
slides.text: A budget is a plan for your money, deciding ahead how much to save and how much to spend. If you get 20 points a week, saving 10 and spending 10 is a simple budget.

slides.title: Different chores, different pay
slides.text: Bigger or harder chores are usually worth more points than quick, easy ones. Cleaning the whole garage might earn more than wiping a table, because it takes more effort.

slides.title: Splitting your allowance three ways
slides.text: You can split your allowance three ways: spend some, save some, and give some. Splitting it up helps you enjoy money now while still planning for later.

slides.title: Keeping track of your money
slides.text: Writing down how much you earn and spend helps you make smarter choices instead of guessing. Keeping a simple list each week can show you when you're saving less than you thought.

slides.title: Setting a savings goal
slides.text: Picking something specific to save for makes saving feel more exciting than saving with no goal at all. If a toy costs 40 points and you save 10 a week, you'll reach it in 4 weeks.

slides.title: Bonus pay for extra effort
slides.text: Some chores might have bonus points if you do them especially well or fast. Bonus pay rewards going above and beyond what was asked.

slides.title: Planning your week's money
slides.text: Before you spend your allowance, think about the whole week ahead. Planning ahead helps you avoid running out of points early in the week.

slides.title: Small goals build big habits
slides.text: Saving for a small goal today builds a habit that helps with bigger goals later. Little goals are good practice for the bigger ones down the road.

quiz.explanation: Bigger or harder chores are usually worth more points than quick, easy ones.

slides.title: Comparing prices
slides.text: The same item can cost different amounts at different stores, so checking first can help your money go further. Comparing prices before buying might save you a few extra points to spend later.

slides.title: Needs, wants, and tradeoffs
slides.text: Even wants can compete with each other, and choosing one over another is called a tradeoff. If you have 20 points, picking a toy or a movie ticket means you can't have both right now.

slides.title: Borrowing and lending
slides.text: Borrowing means using someone else's money now and paying it back later, which means you owe them until it's repaid. Agreeing on when you'll pay a sibling back keeps things fair between you.

slides.title: Spending too fast
slides.text: Spending all your money right away can feel fun, but it can leave you with nothing when something better comes along. Spending every point on payday might mean missing out on a fun reward later that week.

slides.title: Giving and sharing
slides.text: Money isn't just for buying things — you can also give some away to help others. Donating a few points to a friend in need feels good and builds a caring habit.

slides.title: Prices can change over time
slides.text: The cost of things doesn't always stay the same, because prices can go up as time passes. A snack that cost 5 points last year might cost 6 points now.

slides.title: Bigger packs can be a better deal
slides.text: A big bag of chips might cost more than a small bag, but cost less for each chip inside. Checking the size can help you spend smarter.

slides.title: Splitting a cost with a friend
slides.text: If a toy costs more than you have, you and a friend might each pay half. Splitting a cost is sometimes called going in together.

slides.title: Pause before a big purchase
slides.text: Before spending a lot of your money, take a breath and think it over. A short pause can stop a choice you might end up regretting.

slides.title: Price vs. value
slides.text: The price of something is what it costs, but its value is how much it's actually worth to you — sometimes a cheaper item is worth more to you than an expensive one. For example, a $5 book you'll read ten times might be worth more to you than a $20 toy you'll only play with once.

slides.title: Comparing cost per unit
slides.text: When two items look similar, comparing the price per unit — like per ounce or per item — shows which one is actually the better deal. For example, a 10-pack of pencils for $2 costs less per pencil than a 4-pack for $1, even though the 4-pack has a smaller price tag.

slides.title: Not every 'sale' is a real deal
slides.text: Stores sometimes raise a price right before marking it 'on sale,' so a discount doesn't always mean you're actually saving money. For example, a $30 item marked down to $25 after being raised from $20 isn't really a bargain, even though the sign says 40% off.

slides.title: Reading the fine print
slides.text: Sometimes a good deal has hidden costs, like an extra fee or a shorter return window — checking the details before buying avoids surprises. For example, a toy that looks cheaper online might cost more once shipping is added, so checking the full price before deciding avoids a surprise later.

slides.title: Store brand vs. name brand
slides.text: A store's own brand often costs less than a famous name brand, even when the product inside is nearly identical. Trying the cheaper option first can save money without losing much quality.

slides.title: Bulk buying can pay off
slides.text: Buying a bigger size or a multi-pack often lowers the price for each item, but only if you'll actually use it all before it goes bad or gets old. Buying in bulk is only a good deal if nothing goes to waste.

slides.title: Reading a receipt closely
slides.text: A receipt lists every item and fee from a purchase, and checking it can reveal a mistake or a charge you didn't expect. Comparing the receipt to what you actually meant to buy is a useful habit.

slides.title: Extra fees can sneak into a price
slides.text: A shipping fee, service charge, or processing fee can make an item cost more than its listed price. Adding up the true total before buying avoids a surprise at checkout.

slides.title: Return and exchange policies
slides.text: Knowing whether you can return or exchange something before you buy it protects you if it turns out to be the wrong choice. A store with a generous return policy makes trying something new feel less risky.

quiz.explanation: Something's price and its true value to you aren't always the same.

slides.title: Opportunity cost
slides.text: Every time you spend money on one thing, you're giving up the chance to spend it on something else — that trade-off is called opportunity cost. For example, spending your whole allowance on snacks this week means you've given up the chance to put that same money toward a bigger goal, even if you don't notice it in the moment.

slides.title: Avoiding impulse buys
slides.text: An impulse buy is something you buy suddenly, without thinking it through — waiting even one day before a purchase often changes your mind. For example, wanting a toy the second you see it in a store, but deciding to wait 24 hours before deciding, often reveals whether you really wanted it or just got excited in the moment.

slides.title: Budgeting into categories
slides.text: A more detailed budget splits your money into categories, like saving, spending, and giving, instead of just one big pile. For example, splitting 30 points into 15 for saving, 10 for spending, and 5 for giving builds three good money habits at once, instead of just one.

slides.title: Earning money by providing value
slides.text: People usually get paid for doing something useful for someone else — the more value you provide, the more you can reasonably earn. For example, mowing a neighbor's entire yard is worth more than just picking up a few sticks, because it solves a bigger problem for them.

slides.title: Time is a kind of opportunity cost too
slides.text: Choosing to spend an hour on one activity means you can't spend that same hour on something else, just like money. Thinking about both time and money helps you make better choices.

slides.title: The subscription trap
slides.text: A monthly subscription can feel small, but if you stop using it and forget to cancel, you're paying for something you don't even want anymore. Checking your subscriptions regularly avoids wasting money on habit alone.

slides.title: Turning a skill into income
slides.text: A skill you're already good at, like drawing, tutoring, or fixing things, can sometimes be turned into a way to earn money. Thinking about what you're good at can reveal new ways to earn.

slides.title: Negotiating a fair price for a job
slides.text: When you offer to do a job for someone, like walking their dog, it's reasonable to talk about fair pay before you start, not after. Agreeing on pay ahead of time avoids confusion later.

slides.title: Weighing a big purchase against small ones
slides.text: Spending a little bit often on small things can add up to more than one bigger purchase you'd actually value more. Comparing many small buys to one big one can change your decision.

slides.title: Long-term vs. short-term goals
slides.text: A short-term goal might take a few weeks to reach, while a long-term goal — like saving for something big — might take months, and both need different plans. For example, saving 20 points for a small toy might take two weeks, while saving 200 points for a bike might take most of a year, and that longer goal needs more patience and planning.

slides.title: Money and gratitude
slides.text: Being thankful for what you have, instead of always wanting more, tends to make people happier with their money than chasing the next purchase. For example, someone who appreciates the bike they already have tends to feel more satisfied than someone who's already thinking about the next thing to buy the moment they get something new.

slides.title: Giving reflects what you value
slides.text: Choosing to donate part of your money to a cause says something about what matters to you, the same way your spending choices do. For example, someone who cares about animals might set aside a few dollars each month for an animal shelter instead of spending it all on themselves.

slides.title: Reviewing where your money goes
slides.text: Looking back at what you actually spent money on over a month often reveals patterns you didn't notice while spending. For example, checking your spending log might show you spent more on snacks than you realized, which is useful information for planning next month better.

slides.title: Making a plan to reach a goal
slides.text: A goal is more reachable when it's broken into steps, like saving a set amount each week until you reach the total. Breaking a big goal into smaller steps makes it feel less overwhelming.

slides.title: What derails savings goals
slides.text: Small unplanned purchases are one of the most common reasons a savings goal takes longer than expected. Noticing your own spending patterns helps you protect a goal you actually care about.

slides.title: Celebrating progress along the way
slides.text: Noticing progress toward a goal, not just the finish line, can help you stay motivated when saving takes a while. Celebrating being halfway there can keep a long goal feeling worth it.

slides.title: Where your giving goes
slides.text: Money given to a cause, like a shelter or a food bank, is usually used to directly help the people or animals it supports. Understanding where a donation goes can make giving feel more meaningful.

slides.title: Revisiting your goals over time
slides.text: A goal you set months ago might not matter as much to you now, and it's okay to change it. Checking in on your goals occasionally keeps your saving pointed at something you still actually want.

quiz.explanation: Bigger, longer goals typically require more sustained effort and planning.

quiz.explanation: Being thankful for what you have tends to increase satisfaction with money.

slides.title: Skills affect earning potential
slides.text: The more valuable your skills are to others, the more you can typically earn — which is why learning and practicing skills pays off over time, not just in school. For example, someone who learns to code, design, or fix things well often has more ways to earn money than someone with the same amount of free time but fewer developed skills.

slides.title: Net pay vs. gross pay
slides.text: Gross pay is the total amount a job pays before anything is taken out, while net pay is what actually lands in your account after taxes and other deductions. For example, a job that pays $15 an hour might only put about $12 an hour into your account once taxes are subtracted.

slides.title: Where taxes come from
slides.text: A portion of money earned or spent often goes to taxes, which pay for shared things like roads, schools, and public services. For example, part of the price on a receipt at a store is usually sales tax, which goes toward things the whole community uses.

slides.title: Pay yourself first
slides.text: "Paying yourself first" means saving a portion of any money you earn right away, before you spend on anything else, instead of hoping there's something left over. For example, deciding to save 20% of any money earned the moment you get it, before spending on anything, makes saving automatic instead of an afterthought.

slides.title: Different jobs pay different wages
slides.text: Pay often reflects supply and demand: jobs that require rare skills or involve more risk or responsibility tend to pay more than jobs anyone can do with little training. Understanding this can guide which skills are worth developing.

slides.title: Side hustles and freelance work
slides.text: Beyond a traditional job, some people earn money through freelance work or a side hustle, like tutoring, selling crafts, or doing freelance design, often on a flexible schedule. A side hustle can supplement income or help build a skill into something bigger.

slides.title: Understanding a pay stub
slides.text: A pay stub lists gross pay, each deduction like taxes, and the final net pay, giving a full picture of where earned money actually goes. Reading a pay stub carefully is a basic but important financial literacy skill.

slides.title: Automating your savings
slides.text: Setting up an automatic transfer to a savings account each time you're paid removes the temptation to spend that money first. Automating pay-yourself-first turns a good intention into a habit that doesn't rely on willpower.

slides.title: Investing in your own earning potential
slides.text: Spending time or money on a certification, class, or new skill can be a form of investing in yourself, since it can increase what you're able to earn later. Not all valuable investments are purely financial.

quiz.question: How does developing valuable skills affect earning potential?
choices: More valuable skills typically lead to more ways to earn
Skills have no connection to earning money
quiz.explanation: Skills that are useful to others tend to open up more earning opportunities.

quiz.question: What's the difference between gross pay and net pay?
choices: Net pay is what's left after taxes and deductions
They always mean the exact same amount
quiz.explanation: Gross pay is the full amount before deductions; net pay is what you actually receive.

quiz.question: What do taxes generally pay for?
choices: Shared things like roads, schools, and public services
They disappear and pay for nothing
quiz.explanation: Taxes fund shared community resources and services.

quiz.question: What does "pay yourself first" mean?
choices: Saving a portion of money right away, before spending on anything else
Spending everything first and saving whatever happens to be left
quiz.explanation: Paying yourself first makes saving automatic rather than an afterthought.

quiz.question: Why do some jobs pay more than others?
choices: They may require rarer skills or more risk and responsibility
All jobs are required by law to pay the same
quiz.explanation: Pay often reflects how rare the skill is and how much risk or responsibility the job carries.

quiz.question: What is a 'side hustle'?
choices: Extra income earned outside a traditional job, like freelance work
A type of tax that only adults pay
quiz.explanation: A side hustle is extra income earned outside a regular job, often on a flexible schedule.

quiz.question: What does a pay stub show?
choices: Gross pay, deductions, and final net pay
Only how many hours you worked, nothing else
quiz.explanation: A pay stub gives a full picture of gross pay, deductions, and net pay.

quiz.question: Why automate a transfer to savings each payday?
choices: It removes the temptation to spend that money first
Automatic transfers are riskier than doing it manually
quiz.explanation: Automating savings turns a good intention into a reliable habit.

quiz.question: How can learning a new skill be a kind of investment?
choices: It can increase what you're able to earn later
Skills have no effect on future earning
quiz.explanation: Investing time or money in a skill can pay off through higher future earnings.

quiz.question: What connects taxes and net pay?
choices: Taxes are one of the deductions that turn gross pay into net pay
Taxes and net pay are completely unrelated
quiz.explanation: Taxes are deducted from gross pay, which is part of what produces net pay.

slides.title: Credit and debt basics
slides.text: Credit means borrowing money now with a promise to pay it back, often with extra cost added called interest — debt is money you currently owe. For example, buying something on a credit card and not paying it off right away means you'll likely owe more than the original price, because of the added interest.

slides.title: Buy now, pay later has real costs
slides.text: "Buy now, pay later" plans let you get something today and pay for it in smaller pieces, but missing a payment can add fees or hurt your credit. For example, splitting a $200 purchase into four payments feels easier in the moment, but forgetting even one payment can turn a good deal into an expensive mistake.

slides.title: Watching out for recurring costs
slides.text: Small subscriptions or repeating costs can quietly add up to a lot over a year, even if each one feels small by itself. For example, a few small monthly subscriptions that each feel affordable on their own can add up to a genuinely large amount by the end of the year if you never review them.

slides.title: Peer pressure and spending
slides.text: Spending money to keep up with friends or trends can add up fast — it helps to ask whether you actually want something, or just feel like you should have it. For example, buying the newest version of something just because friends have it, even though your current one works fine, is a spending trap worth noticing.

slides.title: Credit scores, briefly
slides.text: A credit score is a number that reflects how reliably someone has repaid borrowed money in the past, and lenders use it to decide who to lend to and at what cost. Building good credit habits early, like paying on time, can matter for years.

slides.title: Interest works both ways
slides.text: Interest can work for you when you save, slowly adding to your balance, or against you when you borrow, slowly adding to what you owe. The same idea can help or hurt you depending on which side of it you're on.

slides.title: Warning signs of a bad deal
slides.text: Pressure to decide immediately, a deal that seems too good to be true, or a plan that's confusing on purpose are all warning signs worth taking seriously. Slowing down is one of the best defenses against a bad financial decision.

slides.title: Lifestyle inflation
slides.text: As income grows, spending often grows right along with it, a pattern called lifestyle inflation, which can quietly prevent someone from ever saving more even while earning more. Noticing this pattern early can help you avoid it.

slides.title: Marketing is designed to influence you
slides.text: Ads and social media are often built specifically to make a product feel necessary or urgent, even when it isn't. Recognizing marketing tactics can help you separate a real need from a manufactured one.

quiz.question: What is credit?
choices: Borrowing money now with a promise to pay it back, often with interest
Money you'll never have to repay
quiz.explanation: Credit involves borrowing with the expectation of repayment, usually plus interest.

quiz.question: What's a real risk of 'buy now, pay later' plans?

quiz.explanation: Missed payments on these plans can lead to fees or credit damage.

choices: Small repeating costs can quietly add up to a lot over a year

quiz.explanation: Multiple small recurring costs can become a large total unnoticed.

quiz.explanation: Pausing to check your real motivation helps avoid spending traps.

choices: How reliably someone has repaid borrowed money in the past
How much cash someone currently has in their wallet
quiz.explanation: A credit score reflects a history of repaying borrowed money reliably.

choices: It can slowly add to your balance when you save

choices: It helps you tell a real need from a manufactured one
Marketing never affects anyone's decisions
quiz.explanation: Recognizing marketing tactics helps you make more intentional spending choices.

choices: Both involve paying later, sometimes with extra cost or risk
Neither one ever involves any risk
quiz.explanation: Both let you get something now while paying later, which carries potential costs or risks.

slides.title: Prices change over time (inflation)
slides.text: The same amount of money often buys a little less over time, because prices tend to rise — that's called inflation, and it's a reason saved money can lose a bit of value if it just sits still. For example, something that cost a certain amount a few years ago often costs noticeably more today, even though nothing about the item itself changed.

slides.title: Emergency funds
slides.text: An emergency fund is money set aside just for unexpected problems, like a sudden expense, so you're not caught without options. For example, having some savings set aside means an unexpected cost, like a broken phone screen, doesn't completely derail your other plans.

slides.title: Thinking in decades, not days
slides.text: Money decisions made consistently over years — saving a little regularly, avoiding debt, spending thoughtfully — tend to matter far more than any single purchase. For example, someone who saves a small, steady amount every month for years often ends up with more than someone who saves in occasional bursts and spends the rest, even if both earned similar amounts overall.

slides.title: Starting to save early pays off
slides.text: Money left in a savings account can earn a small amount of interest over time, and starting even a few years earlier gives that interest more time to build up. For example, saving the same amount starting at 16 instead of 26 gives your money roughly a decade of extra time to grow, even at the exact same savings rate.

slides.title: The real cost of a cheap purchase
slides.text: A cheaper item that breaks quickly and needs replacing can end up costing more over time than a pricier item that lasts, which is sometimes called the total cost of ownership. For example, buying a $10 pair of shoes twice a year can cost more over two years than one $35 pair that lasts the whole time.

slides.title: Compound interest, the short version
slides.text: When saved money earns interest, and that interest starts earning its own interest too, growth can speed up over time — this snowball effect is called compound interest. The earlier money is saved, the longer compound interest has to work.

slides.title: Insurance as a long-term safety net
slides.text: Insurance means paying a smaller, regular amount now so a much larger unexpected cost, like a medical bill or car accident, doesn't fall entirely on you later. It's a long-term way of protecting against a costly surprise.

slides.title: Setting a financial direction, not just a budget
slides.text: A budget manages this month's money, but a financial direction is about where you want to be in five or ten years, and the two should work together. Long-term thinking shapes the smaller decisions made along the way.

slides.title: Small habits compound too
slides.text: Just as money can compound, so can habits — a small, consistent saving habit practiced for years tends to outperform occasional bursts of effort. Long-term financial success is often more about consistency than intensity.
